learningPage.title: What this means
learningPage.explanationText: This is an AI-agent workflow story: AI is being used to help define, run, or supervise a sequence of work instead of only chatting. The teaching angle is control. Once AI can trigger workflows, the key concepts are permissions, sandboxing, auditability, and whether humans can understand what it changed. The main terms to understand are agent, AI capability, model, guardrail, vendor dependency, workflow. Read for the exact job the agent can do, what tools it touches, what permissions it starts with, and what safety controls are named in the story.

This is included in the morning brief because it is dated, source-linked, and matched the scan filters for this section.
articles.emailSummary: A data-center story with possible implications for power demand, grid upgrades, and who pays for capacity.
articles.whyItMatters: This matters because large-load demand can change grid forecasts, trigger upgrade spending, and reopen the question of who pays for capacity.

learningPage.title: What this means
learningPage.explanationText: This is a power-demand story: a large electricity user may change what the utility has to build, forecast, and justify to regulators. The teaching angle is cost allocation. If a data center needs more power or grid upgrades, the important question is whether the company pays or ordinary ratepayers share the bill. The main terms to understand are data center, grid upgrades, ratepayer, large load, utility rates, regulatory review. Read the story by separating three things: the proposed facility, the amount of electricity it may need, and the regulatory/political fight over who pays for infrastructure.

glossary.definition: A large building full of servers. For utilities, it can mean a big new electricity customer that may need grid upgrades.
glossary.whyItMatters: Data centers can consume huge amounts of electricity, so they can change utility forecasts, infrastructure plans, and customer-bill debates.
